blocks.text: The structural unit C=O is the carbonyl group. Aldehydes and ketones are the classes of compounds that contain a carbonyl group: in an aldehyde, RCHO, the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen atom; in a ketone, RCOR', it is joined to two carbon groups. These compounds are abundant in nature and large quantities are made every year. Aldehydes occur in many spices, fruits and natural fragrances; ketones are used in the pharmaceutical, chemical and paint industries. The most common ketone is acetone (propanone), used in nail-polish removers.

blocks.alt: Top left: general aldehyde, C=O with R and H, and ketone, C=O with R and R'. Top right: the carbonyl group labelled flat, sp2, with delta+ on C and delta- on O. Bottom: methanal, an aldehyde and a ketone with an arrow showing reactivity towards nucleophiles increasing from ketone to methanal, because alkyl groups push electrons and crowd the carbon.
blocks.caption: Aldehydes, ketones and the carbonyl group (original diagram after the book's structures).
blocks.long_description: Both aldehydes and ketones contain the polar C=O group. The carbon is slightly positive and is attacked by nucleophiles. Alkyl groups reduce this positive charge and get in the way of the attacking nucleophile, so aldehydes are more reactive than ketones, and methanal, with two hydrogens, is the most reactive.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: The smell and taste of bitter almonds are due to benzaldehyde, C6H5CHO. Acetone (propanone), CH3COCH3, is used in nail-polish removers.

blocks.prompt: What is the difference between an aldehyde and a ketone?
blocks.explanation: In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen (RCHO); in a ketone it is bonded to two carbon groups (RCOR').

items: Aldehyde RCHO (C=O carries H); ketone RCOR' (two C groups).
